newsitem.title: USA: Intervention jitters weaken dollar vs yen.
newsitem.headline: Intervention jitters weaken dollar vs yen.

text.p: NEW YORK, April 16 - The dollar weakened against the yen on Wednesday after remarks by a senior Japanese financial official and the U.S. Trade Representative spurred fresh concern that central banks could intervene to curb any further sharp gains in the dollar.

Senior Japanese Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara warned again that recent movements in the yen-dollar exchange rate were clearly excessive. He also said Japanese authorities will take decisive action at an appropriate time, when they see that intervention can be effective.
Sakakibara, director-general of the Ministry's International Finance Bureau, was speaking to currency dealers in Tokyo.
While U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsy did not directly address the exchange rate, her remarks were also seen as weighing on the dollar.

After a speech during an Economic Strategy Institute conference in Washington, Barshefsky told reporters that the United States is concerned about its trade imbalance with Japan. She stressed that Washington does not wish to see the trade gap grow wider.
On Thursday, the Japanese government will release its customs-cleared merchandise trade surplus for March, while the Commerce Department issues a report on the U.S. trade deficit for February.

A weak yen makes Japanese exports more affordable to foreign buyers and is one factor driving Japan's trade surplus with the United States. Since the beginning of the year, the dollar has risen about 10 percent against the yen.
"It is quite clear that both the U.S. and Japanese goverments want the dollar not to go up further," said Takanobu Igarashi, a senior economist at Sanwa Bank Ltd in New York.

"We don't expect intervention is coming at around this level," said Igarashi, with the dollar trading near 125.60 yen. "But if it goes up further to 127 or 128, then the possibility grows much larger."
In late New York trading, the dollar settled at 125.75 yen, down from 126.07 yen on Tuesday. The dollar rose to 1.7285 German marks, from 1.7270 marks.
In other trading, the dollar climbed to 1.4720 Swiss francs from 1.4670 francs, and to Canadian $1.3972 from C$.1.3970. The British pound fell to $1.6247 from $1.6288.

Nervousness about the possibility of central bank intervention also prompted traders to close out short yen positions against a broad array of currencies. Traders short, or sell a currency they do not own, in anticipation of later being able to purchase the currency at a cheaper price in order to book a profit.
But if traders subsequently fear the currency could strengthen, they rush to purchase the currency to close out the short position and avoid taking a loss.

"People are buying back yen that they previously sold against the European complex, including the mark, Swiss franc and British pound, and also against the dollar," said Marc Chandler, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

John Hazelton, chief foreign exchange dealer at Manufacturers and Traders Bank, said: "I think the major motivation behind people buying the yen is fear of the Japanese and U.S. authorities coming in and intervening, selling dollars and buying yen. So people are trying to protect themselves against that event."
